find: 'English usually puts the subject first (Subject–Verb–Object). Arabic usually starts with the verb (Verb–Subject–Object). So when you translate into Arabic, start with the verb:'

reason: It is a false generalisation that Arabic “usually” starts with the verb: the nominal sentence (جملة اسمية) with SVO order is fully grammatical and very common in MSA; VSO is only the preferred unmarked order in formal writing.

find: 'English always writes _is_ and _are_; Arabic often leaves them out. When _is_ is the main verb, Arabic can use {{يُعدّ}} or {{تُعدّ}}: _Translation is a fascinating field_ → {{تُعدّ الترجمة مجالاً شائقاً}}. Into English, add the verb:
replace: 'In the present tense, English needs _is_ and _are_; Arabic normally leaves them out: _Translation is a fascinating field_ → {{الترجمةُ مجالٌ شائق}}. In formal writing, {{تُعدّ}} (“is considered”) is also possible when the sentence gives an opinion: {{تُعدّ الترجمة مجالاً شائقاً}}. Into English, add the verb:
reason: It presents {{يُعدّ/تُعدّ}} (“is considered”) as the Arabic equivalent of “is”, which adds a meaning and encourages a well-known translationese habit; the normal Arabic equivalent is a nominal sentence without a verb. “When is is the main verb” is also unclear.
